title: Shrinking
synopsis: You're a grieving therapist who has started saying the unsayable thing out loud to your patients. It keeps working. It also keeps blowing up your life. One week. No filter.

nodes.text: Your first patient has spent two years circling the same problem and you, running on bad sleep and worse grief, are about to do the thing they tell you in school never to do: tell him exactly what you think.

choices.text: Tell him to leave his terrible job today
choices.consequence: Some advice is malpractice that happens to work. You commit to tell him to leave his terrible job today. The road to It Worked. Uh Oh. is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

choices.text: Stay professional and let him circle
choices.consequence: The textbook is boring for a reason. You commit to stay professional and let him circle. The road to The Slow Way is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: He quits by lunch and calls you crying with joy. You feel like a genius and a fraud at once. Your mentor Paul appears in your doorway with the face of a man who has heard things. The silence in It Worked. Uh Oh.

choices.text: Tell Paul your new method is brilliant
choices.consequence: Confidence is easy until someone wiser frowns. You choose to tell Paul your new method is brilliant. By Paul's Warning, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

choices.text: Downplay it and promise to be careful
choices.consequence: A small lie to a mentor is a tax you'll repay. You commit to downplay it and promise to be careful. The road to Home, Sort Of is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: You do it right and it's agony — forty-five minutes of careful nudging while the answer sits in the room like a piano nobody will play. He leaves no better. You wonder who the caution is really protecting.

choices.text: Resolve to try the honest way next time
choices.consequence: Patience has limits, and so do you. You commit to resolve to try the honest way next time. The road to Paul's Warning is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

choices.text: Recommit to doing the job properly
choices.consequence: There's wisdom in the boring path too. You commit to recommit to doing the job properly. The road to The Patient You Dread is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: Paul, leaning on his cane and his decades, says, "You're not healing them, you're using them." It stings because it's at least partly true. His Parkinson's tremor is worse today; he hates that you noticed.

choices.text: Ask Paul how he's really doing
choices.consequence: Care him back; he's a patient who refuses to be one. You commit to ask Paul how he's really doing. The road to Home, Sort Of is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

choices.text: Defend your methods to him
choices.consequence: Pride is loudest right before a fall. You commit to defend your methods to him. The road to The Patient You Dread is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: Your daughter Alice is seventeen and grieving her mom in the next room with the door closed. You've been so busy fixing strangers that the most important patient in your life keeps her own counsel.

choices.text: Knock and just listen, no fixing
choices.consequence: Sometimes love is a closed mouth and an open ear. You knock and just listen, no fixing. It gets you to Gaby and the Truth, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

choices.text: Try to fix her grief like a session
choices.consequence: The cobbler's kid has the worst shoes. You choose to try to fix her grief like a session. By Alice's Door Opens, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: Sean, the young veteran with the rage he can't land anywhere safe, has been living in your guest house and your head. He's better and angrier in turns. Today he punched a wall — and almost a person.

choices.text: Push him hard, therapist to friend
choices.consequence: The line between the two is where the work lives. You choose to push him hard, therapist to friend. By Gaby and the Truth, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

choices.text: Give him room and time
choices.consequence: Pressure and patience are both medicines, dosed wrong they're poison. You give him room and time. It gets you to Alice's Door Opens, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: Your colleague Gaby calls you out over coffee: you've been hiding inside everyone else's problems to avoid your own. She's right, she's kind, and she's a little in love with you, which complicates the rightness.

choices.text: Admit she's right about the hiding
choices.consequence: The first honest word is the heaviest. You commit to admit she's right about the hiding. The road to Wednesday Falls Apart is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

choices.text: Deflect with a joke
choices.consequence: Humor is a beautiful place to bury things alive. You commit to deflect with a joke. The road to The Joke That Lands Wrong is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: Alice finally comes out and says the thing: she's furious you got to keep working, keep talking, keep moving, while she had to sit with it. "You help everyone but me," she says, and it lands like a verdict.

choices.text: Apologize without defending yourself
choices.consequence: An apology with a 'but' isn't one. You commit to apologize without defending yourself. The road to Wednesday Falls Apart is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

choices.text: Explain how grief made you useless at home
choices.consequence: The truth, badly timed, can sound like an excuse. You choose to explain how grief made you useless at home. By The Joke That Lands Wrong, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: The patient you told to quit his job calls back — he also told off his wife, his brother, and his landlord, using your name as permission. Your honesty has become a virus with your fingerprints on it.

choices.text: Take responsibility and help him clean up
choices.consequence: You broke it; you don't get to walk away. You take responsibility and help him clean up. It gets you to Paul, In the Hospital, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

choices.text: Tell him he made his own choices
choices.consequence: Half true, fully cowardly. You tell him he made his own choices. It gets you to The Reckoning, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: At the worst possible moment you crack wise and it doesn't land — it wounds. The person you love most looks at you like you're a stranger doing an impression of their dad. The silence after is a long hallway.

choices.text: Drop the act entirely
choices.consequence: Take off the mask before it grows roots. You commit to drop the act entirely. The road to Paul, In the Hospital is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

choices.text: Double down because stopping feels like dying
choices.consequence: Sometimes we defend the very thing that's hurting us. You commit to double down because stopping feels like dying. The road to The Reckoning is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: Paul has a fall. In the fluorescent quiet of the ER he holds your wrist and says the unsayable back to you for once: that he's scared, that he's proud of you, that you have to stop running before grief catches you sitting down.

choices.text: Promise him you'll actually grieve
choices.consequence: A promise to a mentor is a rope you tie to yourself. You promise him you'll actually grieve. It gets you to The Thing You Don't Say, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

choices.text: Tell him to focus on getting better
choices.consequence: Deflection, even now, even here. You choose to tell him to focus on getting better. By The Drive, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: It all arrives at once — Alice, Sean, Gaby, the patient, Paul — every relationship you've been steering with one hand while not looking. Something has to give, and for once it isn't going to be someone else.

choices.text: Call everyone together and come clean
choices.consequence: Radical honesty, finally aimed at the right target: you. You commit to call everyone together and come clean. The road to The Thing You Don't Say is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

choices.text: Disappear for a day to breathe
choices.consequence: Sometimes retreat is the first step of return. You disappear for a day to breathe. It gets you to The Drive, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: You finally say her name — your wife's — out loud, in the present tense and then the past, and the room you've kept locked for a year cracks open. It is the worst and most necessary sentence of the week.

choices.text: Let yourself fall apart in front of them
choices.consequence: Strength and collapse are the same door. You choose to let yourself fall apart in front of them. By Friday, With Alice, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

choices.text: Hold it together for everyone else
choices.consequence: Old habits guard the gate even now. You hold it together for everyone else. It gets you to Sean's Choice, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: You drive nowhere for hours, the way you used to with her. The honesty you've been spraying at everyone turns inward and it's a far harder client to crack. The radio plays her song. You don't change it.

choices.text: Turn the car around and go home
choices.consequence: Home is the one appointment you keep canceling. You choose to turn the car around and go home. By Friday, With Alice, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

choices.text: Keep driving until you understand something
choices.consequence: Some answers only come at sixty miles an hour. You commit to keep driving until you understand something. The road to Sean's Choice is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: Alice finds you at the kitchen table at dawn, both of you wrecked and awake. For the first time you don't try to therapize her. You just say, 'I miss her too, and I'm so sorry I left you alone in it.' She sits down.

choices.text: Grieve with her, no fixing
choices.consequence: Two people in the same wreckage is not nothing. You grieve with her, no fixing. It gets you to The Method, Reconsidered, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

choices.text: Make her breakfast and let the food talk
choices.consequence: Care is sometimes a verb that smells like toast. You commit to make her breakfast and let the food talk. The road to Sunday Light is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: Sean tells you he's moving out — not in anger, but because he's ready. "You fixed me by treating me like family," he says, "which is the one thing they tell you not to do." He's right, and you'd do it again.

choices.text: Let him go with your blessing
choices.consequence: The work is done when they don't need you. You commit to let him go with your blessing. The road to The Method, Reconsidered is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

choices.text: Ask him to stay one more week
choices.consequence: Love and self-interest can wear the same coat. You ask him to stay one more week. It gets you to Sunday Light, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: You sit with Gaby and Paul and admit the honest-therapy experiment was half breakthrough, half breakdown. "Maybe," Paul says, "the trick isn't saying everything. Choose “Adopt Paul's wiser version” and The Right Thing, Kindly comes into view; choose “Insist you'll find your own way” and the road bends toward Family, Chosen and Otherwise.

choices.text: Adopt Paul's wiser version
choices.consequence: Wisdom is honesty that learned some manners. You choose to adopt Paul's wiser version. By The Right Thing, Kindly, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

choices.text: Insist you'll find your own way
choices.consequence: Even the student's mistakes are part of the curriculum. You choose to insist you'll find your own way. By Family, Chosen and Otherwise, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: The week ends quieter than it started. Nobody's cured — that's not how this works — but the people you love are a little less alone, and so are you. The grief is still there. It just isn't driving anymore.

choices.text: Make peace with being a work in progress
choices.consequence: Healing isn't a finish line; it's a practice. You commit to make peace with being a work in progress. The road to The Right Thing, Kindly is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

choices.text: Plan how to do better Monday
choices.consequence: Hope is the homework you assign yourself. You choose to plan how to do better Monday. By Family, Chosen and Otherwise, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: Monday returns, as Mondays do. Your first patient sits down and circles the old problem. This time you wait for the right moment and say the true thing gently — and watch it land like medicine instead of a slap.

choices.text: Trust the kinder honesty
choices.consequence: You finally learned the difference. You choose to trust the kinder honesty. By Saying the True Thing, Kindly, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

choices.text: Check in with Paul afterward, just because
choices.consequence: Gratitude is a session you give for free. You choose to check in with Paul afterward, just because. By For Paul, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: Dinner at your place: Alice, Sean, Gaby, Paul, all the broken beautiful people you accidentally collected. It's loud and imperfect and exactly the kind of mess that means you're alive. Her chair is empty, and that's okay tonight.

choices.text: Raise a glass to the people still here
choices.consequence: Grief and gratitude at the same table. You raise a glass to the people still here. It gets you to The People Still Here, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

choices.text: Slip away to talk to her, one last time this week
choices.consequence: Some conversations don't need a reply. You slip away to talk to her, one last time this week. It gets you to Present Tense, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: You keep the honesty and lose the recklessness, and somehow that's harder and better. Your patients get the truth at a dose they can hold. It isn't a method anymore. It's just you, finally being a good doctor and a worse martyr.

Paul gets better, then worse, then better again, the way bodies do near the end of long good lives. You spend the time. You say the things. When you finally lose him, you've left nothing unsaid — the only kind of goodbye that doesn't haunt you.

The house is full, the wine is cheap, and your daughter is laughing for the first time in months. You built a family out of patients and friends and stubborn love. It's not the family you had. It's the one that saved you.

You talk to her in the dark like you used to, except now you can say her name without flinching. You're not over it. You're through the worst of it, which is the only honest thing grief ever promises. Tomorrow you go to work and help someone else find the door.
